factCheck.evidence: The Sun brightens about 10% per billion years; common estimates put loss of Earth's oceans around 1 billion years out, though some models give 1 to 1.75 billion years, consistent with 'roughly'.

preCheck: Card 002.c2 says 'trillions of them every second'. The real rate is ~10^38 fusion reactions per second, so 'trillions' is a severe understatement. Suggest rewording to 'an enormous number every second' in a new revision.

factCheck.evidence: The claim is accurate: the Sun fuses about 600 million tons of hydrogen into helium each second in its core. (Separately, the card's 'trillions' is far too low; the rate is ~10^38 reactions per second.)

preCheck: Check the page supports "about halfway" / "billions of years more" (NASA commonly gives ~5 billion years remaining).

factCheck.evidence: NASA says the Sun, about 4.6 billion years old, is a little less than halfway through its life and should last about 5 billion more years.

preCheck: Confirm the page says the Sun lacks the mass to go supernova (common NASA statement).

factCheck.evidence: Core-collapse supernovae need stars of at least about 8 solar masses; the Sun lacks the mass and will become a red giant and then a white dwarf.

preCheck: Derived: 30 AU × ~8.3 light-minutes per AU ≈ 4.2 hours. Confirm the page states it or keep as derived.

factCheck.evidence: At Neptune's average distance of about 4.5 billion km (30 AU), sunlight takes about 4.1 hours to arrive.

preCheck: Card says "faint outer glow"; confirm the eclipses page names the corona.

factCheck.evidence: NASA: in totality the Moon blocks the Sun's bright face, leaving the much dimmer corona, the Sun's outer atmosphere, visible.

preCheck: Confirm the 24 h 50 min figure (a lunar day) is on the page.

factCheck.evidence: NOAA says Earth rotates through two tidal bulges each lunar day, giving two high and two low tides every 24 hours and 50 minutes.

preCheck: e.g. John Flamsteed in 1690. Confirm on the page or attach a better source.

factCheck.evidence: Uranus was recorded as a star many times before Herschel's 1781 discovery, e.g. by Flamsteed as '34 Tauri' in 1690 and by Bradley; more than 20 pre-discovery sightings are known.

preCheck: Venera 13 lasted 127 minutes. Confirm.

factCheck.evidence: Venera 7 made the first soft landing in 1970 and later landers followed through 1982; the longest surface survival was Venera 13 at 127 minutes (just over two hours).

preCheck: The distance keeps growing (~23 light-hours in 2026). Confirm the current figure on the page.

factCheck.evidence: Voyager 1's one-way light time exceeded 23 hours in 2025, and NASA says it reaches one light-day (24 hours) on 18 November 2026.

preCheck: Figures vary (~5–15 tons per teaspoon). Card says “several tons”.

factCheck.evidence: Space.com, citing NASA, says a teaspoon of white dwarf matter would weigh about 5.5 tons on Earth.
